findings.problem: The TLDR hardens the one hedged source sentence the entry relies on, in our favour. Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I (verified in the archive.org djvu text, on the page following the printed 855 marker) reads: "Geocentrism's Response: Only light and gases show ether effects; the experiment was incapable of achieving ether detection unless a charged gas is used between the plates." The TLDR reports this as the book calling "that experiment incapable of detecting anything" — the scope (ether detection) is widened to everything and the condition (unless a charged gas is used) is dropped. The refutation and the untraceable block both quote the sentence in full, so this is a summary that outruns its own body, in the field with the highest reader impact, committing on our side the exact drift this project publishes as a finding against the list.
findings.fix: Replace the closing clause with the scoped version, e.g. "— and Galileo Was Wrong, which prints the torsion-balance null a defender would want, answers it by calling the experiment incapable of detecting the ether unless a charged gas is used between the plates." Roughly the same length, and it survives being checked.

findings.field: untraceable (final sentence of the Rowbotham paragraph)
findings.problem: "The refutation above answers that argument, at its own strength, in his own numbers" is false twice over. (a) The refutation contains no answer to Rowbotham's reattribution: searching all published fields, "thermal" and "expansion" occur only in the untraceable block, "Noad", "temperature", "5000" and "39.027" occur nowhere in the refutation, and its only uses of "air" are free-air corrections and aircraft. The arithmetic that would answer him (docstring §3: 188 s/day required, ~24 s/day available on his own 84.2-to-0.0 °F table, short by a factor of ~8; and the London datum he quotes from Noad is defined "in vacuo ... at the temperature of 62°", so temperature and air were held fixed by definition in the very number he is explaining) was researched and never published. (b) "Above" is the wrong direction: render.py places the untraceable block as section 1 and the refutation as section 3. The advocate block's defence against the strongest attack on this entry — that we refuted a phrase nobody wrote — is explicitly built on this missing paragraph, so the gap is load-bearing.
findings.fix: Add the docstring §3 arithmetic to the refutation as a short §2 paragraph in Rowbotham's own numbers (0.170/39.027 = 4.36e-3 → 188 s/day; his Noad footnote gives 8.64 s/day per 30 °F, and his own equator-to-pole span of 84.2 °F yields about 24 s/day; buoyancy over all the air is worth about 6 s/day; and Kater's London figure is by definition reduced to vacuum at 62 °F), then change the untraceable sentence to "The refutation below answers that argument, at its own strength, in his own numbers." If the paragraph is not added, the sentence must be cut, not merely re-pointed.

findings.field: refutation §3 and sources[21] (Wettzell G ring laser)
findings.problem: "the G instrument at Wettzell tracks the Earth's rotation rate to below one part in 10^9, resolving length-of-day variation and polar motion in agreement with VLBI", cited to Eur. Phys. J. C 82 (2022) — Di Virgilio et al., arXiv:2208.09134. The paper supports the first clause (its title is "Overcoming 1 part in 10^9 of earth angular rotation rate measurement with the G Wettzell data" and the Allan deviation drops below 1e-9 after ~1e4 s). It does not support the second: the full text contains zero occurrences of "VLBI" and no occurrence of "length of day", and polar motion appears only as IERS-published Chandler and annual-wobble terms subtracted from the ring-laser data as corrections — corrections the paper itself calls preliminary "since the absolute orientation of the G structure is not known well enough". So the cited paper treats polar motion as an input, roughly the opposite of the independent-confirmation reading our sentence invites. The claim itself is true and documented elsewhere, which makes this a sourcing failure rather than a physics one.
findings.fix: Split the citation: keep EPJC 82 (2022) for the 1-part-in-10^9 stability, and cite the VLBI comparison to its own source (e.g. "Earth rotation variations observed by VLBI and the Wettzell 'G' ring laser during the CONT17 campaign", Adv. Geosci. 50:9, 2019) — or drop "in agreement with VLBI" and say only that the instrument resolves the Earth's rotation rate to below one part in 10^9 with no moving parts, which is all §3 needs.

findings.field: untraceable ("Why this is not filed as older than the movement")
findings.problem: "Instruments this sensitive did not exist before the movement did: the superconducting gravimeter dates from the 1960s, the Cavendish balance from 1798, the Eötvös torsion balance from the 1890s." The sentence is refuted by its own list — 1798 precedes the movement, which this review dates to Rowbotham 1849 (README: "writing 1849-65") — and by the entry's own refutation §2, which rests on Richer's 1672 clock and Kater's 1818 reversible pendulum, i.e. on instruments of exactly the relevant sensitivity, two centuries early. Since a pendulum-clock argument was mechanically available long before the movement, the stated reason for rejecting the pre_modern origin state is the wrong reason, and it sits in the paragraph justifying one of the three origin states the project treats as central.
findings.fix: Rest the paragraph on the correct ground and delete the instrument-dating sentence: "That state records where an argument came from, and it needs an old text that contains the argument. Precision pendulum work is old enough — Richer 1672, Kater 1818 — but no pre-modern text we searched argues from instrument constancy to a stationary Earth, and the gravimeter and the torsion balance postdate the movement's founding texts. There is nothing in the works listed above to inherit from."

findings.problem: Both published fields state that item 252's Moon-tide mismatch is something "the canon's own carriers deny in the sentence next to the one it took" / that "Winship's sentence denies". The located texts say the reverse. On p. 130 of Zetetic Cosmogony — the page immediately before the sentence we quote, and reprinted as "(130-131)" by the Christian Flat Earth Ministry page we cite — Winship writes in his own voice: "But the tides are not uniform. At Port Natal the rise and fall is about six feet, while at Beira, about 600 miles up the coast, the rise and fall is 26 feet. This effectually settles the matter that the moon has no influence on the tides." On p. 131 he prints Melville approvingly: "The Newtonian theory of the Tides does not hold good at Tahiti". And Dubay's proof 118, which the entry's own docstring note 2 records, says flatly "the Earth's tides vary greatly and do not follow the Moon". Our own refutation §5 (line 262) says Winship "treated it as decisive" — so the entry asserts and denies the same thing about the same source. This is the hedge rule inverted: we quoted the concession and stopped where the flat statement sits.
findings.fix: Replace the item-252 paragraph in compression.note with the honest result: "Item 252, “Tidal bores moon visual timing”: this one does not drift on the mismatch. Winship asserts it flatly on p. 130 — “the tides are not uniform…This effectually settles the matter that the moon has no influence on the tides” — prints Melville’s Tahiti observation on p. 131 as proof of it, and Dubay’s proof 118 carries it forward as “the Earth’s tides vary greatly and do not follow the Moon”. What the list drops is the concession Winship attaches on the next page, that the Moon is nonetheless “the TIMEKEEPER for the tides” whose phase “tells what kind of a tide may be expected”, and Scott’s “of this we cannot now be sure”. That is hedge_dropped, not a reversal. Bores are a separate matter: no bore passage is located in any of the tide texts searched for this entry." Amend the gloss sentence at line 206 to match: strike "that Winship's sentence denies" and write instead that Winship asserts the mismatch and concedes the timekeeping in the same two pages.

findings.problem: The authors are wrong. Crossref for the DOI in our own URL (10.1029/2018JC014695) returns Peng, Hill, Meltzner and Switzer — JGR Oceans 124:736-749 (2019). "Peng, Meng and Ge" invents two co-authors, in body prose ("Peng, Meng and Ge examined tide-gauge records worldwide") and again in the source label. Title, journal, volume, first page, year and URL are all correct, so this reads to a defender as a fabricated author list on a page whose entire product is provenance.
findings.fix: Body: "Peng and colleagues examined tide-gauge records worldwide and found that cycle changes high water levels by up to 30 cm." Source label: "Peng, Hill, Meltzner & Switzer, \"Tide Gauge Records Show That the 18.61-Year Nodal Tidal Cycle Can Change High Water Levels by up to 30 cm\", JGR Oceans 124:736-749 (2019)".

findings.field: compression (list_phrasing / source_wording / drift_type / note headline, lines 363-380)
findings.problem: The block's headline finding — "A row its own author scored as non-discriminating arrives on the list as item 245" — depends on identifying item 245, "Tidal resonance geocentric.", with the p. 794 table row, and that identification is asserted with no evidence and one live competitor. The p. 794 cell contains no resonance content of any kind: I searched the item's OCR and "resonan*" occurs on printed pages 633, 634, 809, 855, 864, 872, 875, 876, 888, 906, 965 and 1101 — and not on 794. Pages 633-634 are Hoyle on atmospheric tides in resonance with solar forcing, quoted at length, which is the only tidal-resonance passage located in the book; docstring note 4 spots it and reassigns it to "whichever cluster owns length-of-day" without telling the reader. The entry flags exactly this kind of uncertainty for item 233's "sky torque" and not for 245, and drift_type=force_upgraded for the whole block rests on the unflagged one.
findings.fix: Add to the first paragraph of compression.note, after the p. 820 sentence: "The identification is ours and it is an inference: the row is the only place in the located tide passages where the geocentric literature answers a tidal argument, but the cell says nothing about resonance, and the book's one extended resonance passage — Hoyle on the atmosphere at printed pp. 633–634 — is about tidal braking of rotation and is treated in the length-of-day cluster. If a reader rejects the identification, the consequence is that no source was located for item 245 either, which is a finding of the same weight."

findings.problem: The section is headed "The proposed alternatives, answered on their own hedged terms" and then answers Rowbotham past his hedge. Two problems. First, the prediction attributed to him — "high water simultaneous along the coasts" — is not what he wrote; his stated consequence is "The simultaneous ebb and flow upon meridians 180 degrees apart", which standard theory also delivers. Second, every datum deployed against it falls inside the qualifier our own block quote reproduces four paragraphs earlier: "Whatever peculiarities are observable they may be traced to the reaction of channels, bays, headlands, and other local causes." Holyhaven against London Bridge is an estuary, the St Lawrence and Amazon are rivers — the exact class he scoped out. A defender who has read our own passage quote wins this paragraph.
findings.fix: Rewrite the opening of that paragraph to quote the hedge and answer it: "Rowbotham's stated consequence is narrower than it looks — ‘the simultaneous ebb and flow upon meridians 180° apart’ — and he pre-empts local disagreement by tracing ‘whatever peculiarities are observable’ to ‘channels, bays, headlands, and other local causes’. Take the escape at face value and it costs him the model's only quantitative content: once channel reaction can supply any phase at any place, the floating plane predicts nothing about when high water arrives anywhere, and the prediction it does make in its own voice — a period fixed by the plate's size, ‘once only in about twelve hours’ — is the one that fails, because the period is 12 h 25 min and tracks the Moon." Then keep the Peacock data as illustration of a progressive wave rather than as the refutation. Note that the verdict_challenge reasoning (line 426-429) leans on the same Peacock leg and should be re-worded with it.

findings.problem: The azimuthal-equidistant circumference is computed for 45°N, not 45°S. On a north-polar AE map the 45°S parallel has radius R×135° = 15,013 km and circumference 94,319 km = 50,928 nmi; the published 31,440 km / 16,975 nmi is 2πR(π/4), the 45°N value. So the sentence "22,000 nautical miles is 30% more than the flat azimuthal-equidistant map predicts for that same parallel, which is 16,975 nmi" is wrong by a factor of three AND reversed in direction — 22,000 nmi is 57% BELOW what the disc requires. The conclusion drawn from it, "too big for the globe and too big for the disc", is false on the second half, and the paragraph is introduced as "the check that settles it". advocate.preemptive repeats the error ("the Victorian sailing distances overshoot the flat map by 30% as well") and rests part of the answer to the defender's strongest move on it.
findings.fix: Replace with the correct computation and keep the point, which gets stronger: on the north-polar AE chart the 45°S parallel measures 94,319 km (50,928 nmi), so Rowbotham's 22,000 nmi is 57% SHORT of what the disc demands while being 44% over the globe's 15,282 nmi. Rewrite the conclusion as: his data fit neither model, overshooting the globe and falling far short of the disc — which is what sailing-route distances compared with arcs of a parallel look like. Fix the same number in advocate.preemptive and in docstring 5(c) so the three agree.

findings.problem: The sign-reversal argument does not discriminate, and on the documented track it favours the source. Under uniformly stretched southern parallels the navigator always over-reckons progress along track, which puts an eastbound ship WEST of its DR and a westbound ship EAST of its DR. Milner's ships were eastbound to India (west of DR); Wilkes's Antarctic cruise was westbound — the Vincennes worked the coast from 140°30′E to 112°16′E toward a westward goal of 105°E (United States Exploring Expedition, Jan–Feb 1840) — so "consistently east of his reckoning" is the SAME along-track error as Milner's and is precisely what Carpenter's and Rowbotham's model predicts. The text asserts the opposite ("Errors that reverse sign … are what local currents look like, not what a rescaled globe looks like") and presents it as "the discriminating detail". It also locates Wilkes in the Drake Passage, which neither Dubay's item nor the expedition record supports for that report.
findings.fix: Delete the sign-reversal claim and replace it with the argument that actually works: a stretched-parallel model predicts a fixed FRACTIONAL over-reckoning that grows monotonically with southern latitude and is identical on every heading and every day, whereas the reported errors are intermittent, vary with locality and season, and reverse relative to heading — the signature of set and drift. If the current line is kept, note that the Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows eastward and so displaces a ship east of DR regardless of heading, which fits Wilkes's report directly; and state Wilkes's actual working ground (Wilkes Land, roughly 100–160°E) rather than the Drake Passage.

findings.problem: The words "consistently east of his reckoning, sometimes over 20 miles in less than 18 hours" are quoted as Wilkes's ("Wilkes recorded being …", "Wilkes's reported 20 miles of unaccounted easting"). They are Dubay's, from 200 Proofs item 37 ("in his journals also mentioned being consistently east of his reckoning…"). The docstring gets the provenance right ("Dubay 37 has Wilkes…"); the published text does not. Wilkes's Narrative was not consulted, so a secondary summary is presented as a primary record and then used as the empirical anchor of both the steelman and the sign argument. On a project whose product is provenance this is the worst available place for it.
findings.fix: Attribute the quotation to Dubay and scope what was checked: "Dubay's proof 37 reports that Wilkes 'mentioned being consistently east of his reckoning, sometimes over 20 miles in less than 18 hours'; the wording is Dubay's and was not located in Wilkes's Narrative of the United States Exploring Expedition, which was not reached for this entry." Then say the argument does not depend on the attribution being right.

findings.field: clusters.py B12 originator (renders as the meta line) vs passage.gloss and people[]
findings.problem: clusters.py credits Charles K. Johnson, Flat Earth News, 1972, and render.py emits "· first published by Charles K. Johnson" on the summary line next to the verdict chip. Directly beneath it the gloss calls Carpenter 1885 "the earliest text located that states this cluster's argument in numbered-proof form", quotes Rowbotham 1865 as earlier prose, and people[] lists Rowbotham/Carpenter/Dubay with no Johnson. "Earliest text located" and "first published by Johnson (1972)" cannot both be true on the same card. The docstring says twice that this was "reported up in record_problems" — but there is no record_problems key in _b11_B12.py, no batch-11 report in review/, and a grep for B12 across review/ returns only triage.json. This is recurring failure #5 (clusters.py contradicts the entry) compounded by #4 (a fix described as done that has not landed anywhere).
findings.fix: Either add the record_problems array this file's docstring promises, or file the defect in review/ where the batch report will read it: B12 originator=Charles K. Johnson is unverified, no Johnson text carrying a navigation argument was reached, and the documented chain is Rowbotham 1865 → Carpenter 1885 → Dubay 2015. Until the field moves, withdraw to untraced rather than substituting another guess (README's three-state rule), and do not leave the entry asserting an ancestry the meta line contradicts. Also note the cluster note ("Antarctic circumnavigation and the 24-hour midnight sun…") describes an argument this treatment never makes.

findings.problem: The quote is truncated mid-sentence, without a trailing ellipsis, at the exact clause that reverses its force. Both scans read: "As it stands, there was a lot of room to make adjustments to Ptolemy's model to fit the observations, but no one was willing to do so ONCE COPERNICUS' SYSTEM WAS SEIZED AND PROMOTED BY THE RENAISSANCE AND ENLIGHTENMENT AS A MEANS TO DEMOTE THE AUTHORITY OF SCRIPTURE AND TAKE CONTROL AWAY FROM THE CATHOLIC CHURCH TO INFLUENCE THE MINDS OF MEN." We stop at "do so", present the remnant as a concession in the book's own voice (gloss: "the adjustments... were never made"; refutation section 2: "the book's own next move is to say the note was never redeemed"), and then answer the deleted clause in the TLDR ("The model was not put down by decree") without ever showing the reader that the source states it. The seventh edition sharpens the same claim two lines earlier: "Copernicus... chose not to make those adjustments and instead wanted to throw the baby out with the bath water." This is the hedge rule violated on our side, in the field the reader treats as the source's own words, on a page whose entire premise is that truncation is the offence.
findings.fix: Mark the truncation and disclose the rest. The 57-word quote is at the 60-word cap, so trim the first sentence to "before Kepler's improvements to the heliocentric model, Copernicus' system was no more accurate than Ptolemy's" and end the second with "...but no one was willing to do so ..." with a visible ellipsis; then add one gloss sentence: "The sentence does not end there. It continues 'once Copernicus' system was seized and promoted by the Renaissance and Enlightenment as a means to demote the authority of Scripture' - so this is not a concession that the model failed but a claim that it was abandoned for non-scientific reasons, and that claim is what the chronology below answers."
